# The April 2026 meeting, as a corpus

::: {.di-lede}
The April 23–24, 2026 TAC meeting produced a one-page agenda, five presentation artifacts, and
nine pages of summary minutes. This site turns that material into something a committee can
actually use between meetings — and argues that the whole TAC cycle should work this way.
:::

## The two documents

::: {.di-cards .di-cards-2}
::: {.di-card}
### [A Fuller Record](documents/meeting-summary-2026-04.qmd)

A comprehensive summary of the April meeting, organised by issue rather than by clock.
Built from the official minutes treated as a rough transcript, plus everything the minutes
could not carry — the findings locked in chart images, the eight hidden slides, the two
speaker notes, and the participation total the handout never prints.

Written as a deliberate contrast to the official minutes.

[HTML](documents/meeting-summary-2026-04.qmd) · [PDF](documents/meeting-summary-2026-04.pdf)
:::

::: {.di-card}
### [Toward an AI-Native TAC](documents/ai-native-tac.qmd)

A brief for Andrew Middlestead, Director of the Office of Educational Assessment and
Accountability, on what changes if the committee's work is captured, structured, and carried
forward as a corpus rather than as a document.

Part I makes the case. Part II is the technical appendix for whoever would build it.

## The corpus

The [corpus index](wiki/index.md) is the way in. A few useful entry points:

- **[Open recommendations](wiki/recommendations/open-recommendations-april-2026.md)** — the
  register. What the committee advised, to whom, and where each item stands. This is the page a
  working meeting should be run against.
- **[The meeting](wiki/meetings/2026-04-23-tac-meeting.md)** — roster, sessions, and the thread
  running through them.
- **[Glossary](wiki/glossary.md)** — AGP, NGA, CT-PO, QWK, MTTC, and the rest.

Standing topics outlive any one meeting and are the unit of institutional memory:
[adequate growth targets](wiki/topics/adequate-growth-targets.md),
[subscore reporting](wiki/topics/m-step-subscore-reporting.md),
[MTTC form security](wiki/topics/mttc-meaningfully-different-forms.md),
[interim adoption](wiki/topics/smarter-balanced-interim-adoption.md).

## Why bother

::: {.di-editorial}
The official minutes are competent. They are also lossy in ways that are specific and
measurable: every question and every recommendation is attributed to "TAC" rather than to any of
the five members present; a correlation is reported as "between 2.7 and 2.8"; the substance of a
52-page simulation study reduces to a single sentence because it lives in pictures; and material
that exists only in speaker notes — including the repeal of educator evaluations from state law —
never surfaces at all.

None of that is a failure of drafting. It is what happens when a two-day technical conversation
has to become a nine-page document three weeks later, written by one person, with no way to
represent a figure.
:::

The alternative is not a better document. It is a different artifact: a corpus that any
participant — or any agent working on their behalf — can query, that carries advice forward with
its status attached, and from which documents are *generated* rather than authored.

This site is that alternative, built from the material we actually have.

::: {.callout-note}
## On the source material

This corpus is built from the April 2026 summary minutes treated as a stand-in for a transcript,
because no transcript exists. Where the minutes attribute a question or a recommendation to the
committee as a body rather than to a person, that attribution is preserved — inferring who said
what would fabricate a record the source cannot support. That gap is the clearest single argument
for capturing the next meeting properly.
:::
